beats.care: Healthy wildlife keeps diseases in check. The Hindu wants every state to have a recovery plan.
beats.what: Asiatic lions grew from 674 to 891, and Madhya Pradesh's vultures from 8,397 to 12,981.
beats.why: A toxic cattle drug was banned, and breeding and habitat protection helped species recover.

cards.body: Rare good news: Asiatic lions grew from 674 in 2020 to 891 in 2025. Vultures in Madhya Pradesh rose from 8,397 in 2019 to 12,981 in 2025.
The piece argues extinction isn't always final. When scientists, governments and local communities work together, species recover.
cards.title: From the brink to a comeback, hope for India's wildlife
cards.verdict: Its ask: turn these one-off wins into a national plan, with clear targets for every state.

cards.body: Vultures ate dead cattle that had been given diclofenac, a painkiller that destroyed their kidneys. Banning it for animals, plus breeding programmes and protecting their homes, helped them recover.
cards.title: why did vultures almost disappear?

cards.body: Vultures clean up dead animals, which stops diseases spreading to people. And India holds about 8% of the world's plants and animals on just 4% of its land, so what happens here matters for the whole planet.
Only about 2% of India's known animal species have even been checked for extinction risk. Of the 7,516 checked, 1,012 are threatened.

cards.q: What nearly wiped out India's vultures?
cards.why: Diclofenac, used on cattle, poisoned vultures that fed on the carcasses.
